sections.heading: Why Do So Many Students Stall on MYP Physics Criterion B and C?
paragraphs: Students stall on Criterion B and C for two reasons operating at once: physics content becomes genuinely cumulative from around Year 4 onward, and the assessment format simultaneously shifts toward demanding independent reasoning rather than straightforward recall of facts and formulae. A shaky grasp of vectors in one term undermines work on forces in equilibrium a term later, which then undermines circular motion the term after that, and so the gap compounds quietly across an academic year rather than announcing itself in any single test. Students rarely announce this gap directly to a parent; instead they compensate by memorising formula triggers without the underlying reasoning behind them, which works fine until a question is phrased slightly differently from the one they practised repeatedly at school.

The move to inquiry-based assessment adds a second layer of difficulty that has comparatively little to do with physics knowledge on its own — it sits closer to a writing and reasoning skill than a science one. A student can understand momentum conservation perfectly well in conversation and still lose real marks on Criterion C because their written evaluation paragraph simply lists what went wrong in the experiment without explaining how each limitation actually affected the numerical result they obtained. This distinction between describing a limitation and properly evaluating its impact is genuinely subtle, and it is rarely taught explicitly inside a classroom of twenty-five students working through a fixed syllabus timetable with limited time for individual feedback. One Wazirabad parent described a child who scored well on every Criterion A test that year yet still lost real marks on a first investigation, simply because nobody had explained what a justification paragraph needs to include.

Requests for an IB MYP Physics crash course in Gurugram spike noticeably around late Year 4 and early Year 5, usually once a first personal investigation draft comes back from school with feedback the student cannot fully parse or act on alone. Parents describe a child who clearly understood the physics discussed in class but froze when asked to justify a choice of apparatus or defend a particular sample size in writing, because nobody had previously asked them to defend a methodological decision out loud, let alone on paper under a word limit. A tutor who has seen this pattern before can usually tell within the first ten minutes of a diagnostic conversation whether the gap is genuinely about content or purely about how to write up a defence of a method under a fixed word count.

One honest limitation is worth stating plainly here rather than glossing over it: a tutor cannot manufacture genuine interest in an investigation for a student who simply dislikes practical science, and forcing enthusiasm tends to backfire visibly within a session or two. What a good tutor can realistically do instead is make the entire process procedural and considerably less anxiety-inducing — a repeatable approach to any investigation prompt the school sets, rather than reinventing the wheel from a blank page every single time a new one is assigned partway through term. Framing the process this way — as a checklist to work through rather than a creative leap to make from nothing — tends to lower the anxiety considerably, even for a student who will never find circuits or pendulums intrinsically fascinating.

sections.heading: What Does the IB Primary Years Programme Actually Assess in Years 1 to 6?
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme is organised around six transdisciplinary themes — who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet — each explored through a unit of inquiry that deliberately blends maths, language and science together rather than teaching them as separate, isolated subjects on a fixed timetable. The learner profile attributes — inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, knowledgeable, principled, caring, open-minded, balanced and reflective — run through every single unit as shared vocabulary between school and home, and children are regularly asked to reflect on which of these attributes they actually used during a given piece of work. A tutor who genuinely understands this shared language can help a child articulate that reflection honestly, rather than simply reaching for whichever attribute sounds most impressive on the page. It is a small, specific skill, but a meaningful number of Year 4 and Year 5 students in Ansal Esencia visibly struggle with it when asked to write such a reflection entirely unprompted.

Year 6 brings the PYP exhibition, a term-long, genuinely student-led inquiry into a real-world issue that culminates in a public presentation to the wider school community, usually the single heaviest piece of independent work a PYP student produces before moving on to the Middle Years Programme (MYP). This is also where families most often ask for a tutor, not to actually do the research on the student's behalf, but to help a child manage a genuinely open-ended, multi-week project with no single correct answer waiting at the end of it. Pacing the exhibition correctly across an entire term matters considerably more than any single session's content, and rushing it into the final fortnight almost always produces a visibly thinner presentation than one built up gradually from an early start.

Assessment across the PYP is continuous rather than exam-based, which is precisely why the programme uses no formal grade scale comparable to IB Diploma Programme (DP) scores of 1 to 7, or the 9-1 and A*-G scales used in IGCSE. Instead, a child's development is tracked through portfolio evidence, teacher observation notes and the learner profile reflections gathered across each unit, then reported to parents through a structured narrative rather than a single number. sections.heading: Why Is Supporting IB PYP Inquiry at Home Harder Than It Looks?
paragraphs: The PYP's biggest risk at home is not that a child quietly falls behind on content — it is that well-meaning help slides gradually into doing the thinking for them instead. A parent or tutor under time pressure on a Tuesday evening will often simply answer the question a child was actually meant to investigate themselves, because that is faster and less frustrating for everyone at the table. Over a full term this genuinely adds up to a child who can produce a tidy, well-formatted inquiry journal but cannot properly explain how they arrived at a conclusion when the class teacher asks directly in conference. This gap tends to surface at the worst possible moment, during a live classroom discussion rather than in the relative safety of a home session where an adult can quietly step in.

The opposite failure is just as common in practice, and arguably harder to notice: leaving a child entirely unstructured because inquiry-based sounds like it should mean no guidance at all from an adult. Some Ansal Esencia parents describe a child staring blankly at a research prompt for thirty or forty minutes with no real progress made, not because the topic itself is too difficult but because nobody has actually shown them how to break one large, open question into two or three smaller, genuinely answerable ones first. That is a specific, teachable skill in its own right, not a fixed personality trait a child either has or lacks, and it tends to improve noticeably once a tutor models the process aloud a handful of times.

A tutor's real value across the PYP years is holding exactly that middle ground consistently — asking the next question rather than simply supplying the next answer, and knowing the difference between a moment when a child genuinely needs a fact explained and a moment when they simply need thirty seconds of silence to think it through on their own. This is considerably harder to do well than straightforward subject tutoring at older grades, and it is fair to say plainly that not every tutor who is genuinely strong at Class 10 board coaching turns out to be equally good at this particular style of guided questioning, which is exactly why IB Gram treats PYP matching as a separate specialism rather than an extension of older-grade tutoring.

One honest limitation is worth naming directly here: a tutor cannot manufacture curiosity in a child who is simply tired, overstimulated by a packed after-school schedule, or going through a difficult week at school unrelated to academics at all. What a good tutor can do instead is keep sessions short enough, and specific enough to the child's actual current unit, that even a low-energy Tuesday evening still produces some small, genuine forward movement rather than a session that both child and tutor quietly write off as wasted. Naming this limitation directly, rather than pretending every session can be equally productive regardless of how the child's day has gone, tends to build more trust with a family over time than a tutor who promises steady progress no matter what.

sections.heading: What Does the IB Primary Years Programme Actually Ask a Young Learner to Do?
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme asks a child to build understanding through structured inquiry rather than through memorising a fixed body of facts, working across six transdisciplinary themes that recur every year at increasing depth: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. A single unit of inquiry typically runs for several weeks and pulls maths, language and science into one connected investigation rather than teaching each as a separate period on the timetable, which is precisely the structure a worksheet-based tutor tends to flatten back into isolated subjects without meaning to. A parent watching a session for the first time often needs this pointed out directly, since a blended lesson can look, at a glance, like it is simply wandering off-topic when it is actually following the unit exactly as designed.

Running alongside every unit is the learner profile, ten attributes — inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, knowledgeable, principled, caring, open-minded, balanced, reflective — that a school treats as seriously as academic content when tracking a child's development across the year. A parent unfamiliar with the PYP often assumes these are soft, optional extras layered on top of the real work, when in practice a class teacher weighs them directly into how a child's progress gets reported at the end of each term. A tutor who never mentions the learner profile across a whole term of sessions is likely missing half of what the school is actually paying attention to, and it is fair to ask directly how they plan to touch on it.

The programme's centrepiece arrives in Year 6 with the PYP exhibition: a self-directed, collaborative investigation into a real issue the students themselves select, researched in groups over an entire term and presented publicly to the wider school community. It is typically the single largest piece of independent work a child produces before leaving primary school, and it rewards precisely the inquiry habits — or exposes precisely the gaps — that were built, or left unbuilt, across the five years before it. A child who has spent those years being told the answer rather than asked the question typically finds the exhibition's open-endedness genuinely disorienting at first, which is exactly why the groundwork laid in earlier years matters so much.

Because assessment runs continuously through portfolios, teacher observation and the exhibition itself rather than a scheduled exam, the PYP carries no numbered grade scale comparable to the International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma Programme's 1 to 7 scores, or the 9-1 and A*-G scales used at IGCSE level. A family moving into Bestech Park View City from a more exam-driven school system often needs this explained plainly in the first conversation, since a first PYP report reads unlike anything an older sibling brought home. A tutor who explains this scoring difference early on tends to save a family a fair amount of needless worry over a report that was never designed to carry a single grade in the first place.

sections.heading: Why Is Guiding PYP Inquiry at Home Harder Than Parents Expect?
paragraphs: Guiding PYP inquiry at home is harder than it looks because the instinctively helpful move — explaining an answer clearly so a struggling child can move on — is exactly the move the programme wants a tutor to resist. A multiplication table genuinely benefits from repetition and correction. A unit of inquiry does not; the school wants a child arriving at understanding through their own questioning, so a tutor who supplies the conclusion first, however well-intentioned, is quietly undoing the exact skill the class teacher spent the week building. It takes real discipline for an adult to sit through a child's slow, halting attempt at reasoning without stepping in early, and that discipline is exactly what separates a genuinely good PYP tutor from an otherwise capable one.

A second, less obvious difficulty is that PYP content simply will not sit still. A tutor cannot master one syllabus and reuse it term after term the way a board-exam tutor reasonably can, because the transdisciplinary theme changes every few weeks and each new unit demands fresh, specific background reading before a session can be planned properly. Supporting how the world works this term and how we organise ourselves the next calls for a tutor genuinely comfortable improvising inside an inquiry framework, which is a different and less common skill from delivering fixed content reliably. Tutors who have only ever taught a fixed board syllabus sometimes struggle with this shift more than a parent expects, even when their subject knowledge itself is genuinely strong.

There is a real failure mode on the opposite side as well, and it deserves equal attention. An inquiry-based approach applied too loosely, with no scaffolding at all, can leave a young child genuinely directionless rather than curious, staring at an open prompt with no sense of where to begin. The honest middle path is guided questioning with enough structure that a session still produces something concrete by the end of it, not an unstructured conversation that feels pleasant but goes nowhere. A parent can usually tell the difference within a session or two simply by asking the child afterward what they actually worked out for themselves that day, rather than what the tutor told them.

One limitation is worth naming without softening it: a tutor cannot manufacture genuine interest in a topic a child simply finds dull that week, and forcing enthusiasm tends to read as false to a child faster than most adults expect. What a good tutor can do instead is connect even an unloved topic to something the child already cares about, which is a modest, achievable goal compared with trying to make every single unit equally exciting. Naming a dull week honestly, rather than pretending enthusiasm that is not really there, tends to keep a child's trust in the process over the long run and makes the genuinely interesting weeks land better by contrast.

sections.heading: What Does the IB Primary Years Programme Syllabus Actually Cover?
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme sits at the start of the International Baccalaureate continuum, before the Middle Years Programme (MYP) and the Diploma Programme (DP) come later, and it is organised around six transdisciplinary themes: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. Each theme anchors a unit of inquiry lasting several weeks, built around a central idea with two or three lines of inquiry underneath it, and there is no fixed textbook chapter a tutor can simply open; the unit itself functions as the syllabus for that stretch of term.

Running alongside the six themes is the learner profile: ten attributes, inquirer, knowledgeable, thinker, communicator, principled, open-minded, caring, risk-taker, balanced and reflective, that schools use as shared vocabulary for describing how a student is growing, not only what they currently know. A tutor unfamiliar with this vocabulary ends up speaking a different language from the school report, which is confusing for a child trying to connect a tutoring session with what their teacher says in class. Asking a prospective tutor to name which attribute your child is currently strongest on is a fair, quick way to test whether they actually know the framework.

For Grade 6 students, the PYP exhibition is the culminating piece of the entire programme: a self-directed, often group-based inquiry into a real-world issue, researched over most of a term and presented to the wider school community. It is the single biggest source of PYP-related tutoring requests we see from families in this corridor, largely because it demands research skills and time management most ten- and eleven-year-olds have never had to apply independently before. There is no numeric or letter grade scale at PYP level the way the DP uses a 1-7 scale later; the exhibition is assessed through the learner profile and reflection, not a mark sheet.

A concrete example helps: a Grade 6 student exploring 'how we organise ourselves' might choose waste segregation in a housing society as an exhibition topic, then need to narrow that broad theme into an investigable question, plan several weeks of research and interviews, and structure a final presentation, largely without an adult doing the thinking for them. A tutor's honest role here is coaching the process, narrowing a question, planning a research timeline, structuring a presentation, rather than supplying the project's content, since a PYP exhibition that reads as adult-written defeats its own purpose.

sections.heading: What Does the IB Primary Years Programme Actually Teach, Year by Year?
paragraphs: The PYP is built around six transdisciplinary themes: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. Each year a child moves through several units of inquiry built on these themes, and each unit runs for a few weeks around a single central idea with two or three lines of inquiry underneath it. There is no fixed textbook chapter to point to; the unit itself is the syllabus.

Running alongside the six themes is the learner profile: ten attributes, inquirer, knowledgeable, thinker, communicator, principled, open-minded, caring, risk-taker, balanced, reflective, that get assessed inside the unit itself rather than on a separate test. A tutor helping with PYP needs to say, concretely, which of these a child is strong on and which one needs work this term, because that is the language the school itself is using in its own reports.

The one fixed milestone in the programme is the PYP exhibition, typically in the final year of primary schooling (Grade 5 or 6 depending on how a school numbers it): a student-initiated, collaborative inquiry into a real issue, researched and presented to the wider school community over most of a term. It is meant to be led by the students, not by adults handing them content, so the honest role for outside support is research skills, time management and presentation structure, not writing the project itself.

A worked example from this corridor: a student exploring 'how the world works' might investigate water conservation in a local society, needing to design a small survey, interview a facilities manager, and present findings with a recommendation. A tutor's job is coaching each step, how to phrase a survey question that actually yields useful answers, how to structure an interview, how to turn raw notes into a presentation, rather than handing the child a finished project dressed up to look student-made.

Every unit has a central idea and several lines of inquiry

sections.heading: Is Online Tutoring Actually Better Than Home Visits for PYP in DLF Phase 4?
paragraphs: For some parts of PYP, yes, online is genuinely just as good and often more convenient, and for other parts, no, home wins clearly. Online tutoring is fine for the parts of PYP that look like traditional learning: phonics, reading fluency, times tables, and talking through a unit's central idea out loud. A tutor on a screen can hold a child's attention for these just as well as one sitting beside them, and scheduling is far easier when MG Road traffic is the alternative.

It is weaker for the parts that need a body in the room. A Year 1 or Year 2 child building a model, sorting physical objects for a science-based unit, or simply needing someone to sit close while they write, tends to do better with someone physically present. Screen fatigue shows up faster in six- and seven-year-olds than in teenagers, and PYP leans on hands-on tasks more than any later stage of the IB does.

Set out plainly: home tutoring wins for younger children and hands-on model-building but costs travel time through MG Road traffic; online tutoring wins on convenience and works fine for reading, discussion and exhibition research but loses ground with a child under eight who needs a physical presence to stay engaged; a hybrid pattern, home in exhibition-heavy terms and online for routine practice weeks, works for most DLF Phase 4 families we have matched, avoiding MG Road travel time on every single session while keeping hands-on weeks in person.

So the honest answer changes with age. Under Year 3, home sessions usually earn their cost. From Year 4 or 5 onward, the hybrid pattern above works for most families, and some parents choose online for the entire arrangement simply because a reliable evening slot matters more to them than physical presence, a fair trade once a child is old enough to hold focus through a video call without constant redirection.

sections.heading: Why the IB PYP Is Trickier to Tutor Than a Normal Subject
paragraphs: There is no syllabus PDF to work through, which sounds freeing until you realise it is also the main way PYP tutoring goes wrong. Without a fixed content list, a tutor under pressure to show visible progress will quietly default to worksheets and correct-answer drilling, the opposite of what the programme is trying to build. It is an easy trap, and not always an obvious one from the outside, even to a well-meaning parent watching the session unfold.

Progress also does not show up the way a parent might expect. There is no weekly test score to track. What you are looking for instead is whether your child is asking better questions, taking more risks with an idea, or reflecting on their own work with less prompting, approaches-to-learning skills, in the programme's own terms. That is a harder thing to report on than a mark out of ten, and it asks more of the tutor's own vocabulary than most subject tutoring does.

A tutor trained mainly in CBSE or ICSE primary teaching can still do this well, but it is not automatic. Ask directly how they would extend this week's unit rather than just support it, whether they plan an activity that pushes the central idea further, or simply reinforce what the school already covered. The answer tells you more about actual fit than the résumé does, and it takes about two minutes to ask in a first conversation.

sections.heading: What Is Actually in the IB Primary Years Programme Syllabus?
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme is organised around six transdisciplinary themes, who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet, each explored through a unit of inquiry that blends subjects rather than teaching them separately. A parent used to a subject-by-subject school report can find this structure genuinely confusing at first, since a single unit might touch literacy, science and social studies together within the same few weeks.

The learner profile, attributes like inquirer, thinker, communicator and risk-taker among ten total, runs alongside academic content and is assessed as part of how a child engages with learning, not as a separate subject. This means a tutoring session that only drills reading or maths in isolation, disconnected from the current unit, is missing part of what the school itself is actually assessing that term.

By the final year, the PYP exhibition asks students to identify a real-world issue, research it collaboratively, and present their inquiry to the school community, drawing on everything the learner profile and transdisciplinary skills were meant to build over the previous years. It is less a test of content knowledge and more a test of whether a child can drive their own inquiry, precisely the skill hardest to support with traditional tutoring methods built around answers and correction.

A worked example: a student exploring 'sharing the planet' might investigate plastic use in the school canteen, needing to gather simple data over two weeks, compare it against a stated goal, and propose one realistic change. sections.heading: Why the IB Primary Years Programme Is Harder to Tutor Than It Looks
paragraphs: Parents moving a child into the Primary Years Programme from a more conventional system often assume tutoring means catching up on missed content. It rarely is. The Primary Years Programme does not hand a tutor a fixed syllabus of facts to revise; it organises learning around six transdisciplinary themes — who we are, how we express ourselves, how the world works, where we are in place and time, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet — and expects a child to build understanding through inquiry inside each one across the year. A tutor who defaults to explaining a fact and testing recall is working against the structure of the programme, not reinforcing it, however strong their subject knowledge otherwise is.

The learner profile makes this genuinely harder. PYP reports a child against ten attributes — inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, knowledgeable, principled, caring, open-minded, balanced and reflective — alongside subject skills, so a tutor has to notice and name when a student is being reflective or taking a reasonable risk with an idea, not only when a maths answer comes out right. That is an unfamiliar skill for a tutor trained on CBSE or ICSE-style drilling, and it is the main reason PYP tutoring needs someone who has actually worked inside an IB classroom or with PYP students specifically. Many DLF Wellington Estate schools carry PYP students directly into the Middle Years Programme (MYP) from Class 6, so the inquiry habits built now do not reset at that point.

The exhibition in Year 6 raises the stakes further, and it deserves honest framing rather than being treated as just another assignment. It is a self-directed, largely student-led inquiry into a real-world issue, researched over several weeks and presented to the whole school community, drawing on every learner profile attribute and inquiry skill built up over the preceding five years. A child who has spent those years being told the right answer can struggle badly with the blank page the exhibition demands once preparation typically begins for a Term 2 or Term 3 presentation. Tutoring support here has to build the muscle of independent thinking gradually, unit by unit, rather than attempting to teach it in the final term.

There is also a risk worth naming plainly: a tutor who is too directive can do more harm than one who does too little, because PYP explicitly assesses the process of inquiry, not just the polish of the final output. A parent who wants visible, fast progress can end up pushing for a tutor who supplies answers quickly, which produces a tidier worksheet but a child who has practised being told rather than practised thinking. IB Gram is upfront with families about this tension during matching, because the tutors who produce the best long-term results in PYP are often the ones whose sessions look, on the surface, slower and less structured than a CBSE-style tuition class.

sections.heading: What Does the IB PYP Syllabus Actually Cover in DLF Wellington Estate?
paragraphs: The IB PYP syllabus is not a syllabus in the conventional sense — there is no fixed textbook chapter list, only six transdisciplinary themes repeated with growing depth each year, and each unit of inquiry built around a central idea, lines of inquiry and key concepts such as form, function, causation or change that a child applies in their own words. Schools in this cluster, including Lancers International and Pathways World, do not always sequence the same theme in the same term, so a tutor working with a DLF Wellington Estate family needs to confirm the current unit before a session, not assume it from the child's age alone.

Literacy and numeracy sit alongside the units rather than inside a separate subject box. A Year 3 reading session might tie directly into a 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit on community systems, and a maths session on data handling might grow out of a 'Sharing the Planet' unit on resources and sustainability. A tutor who treats reading and maths as standalone subjects misses this connection entirely, and a child's schoolwork starts to feel like two unrelated worlds instead of one integrated inquiry — precisely the confusion many DLF Wellington Estate parents describe when they first call about a mismatch with a previous tutor.

Assessment in PYP is genuinely continuous rather than test-based, which is the detail that drives the whole tutoring timetable. Teachers gather evidence through portfolios, structured observation, student self-assessment and reflection journals across a unit, rather than a single end-of-unit paper, so there is no fixed date to revise toward the way a board exam creates one. That changes what a tutor should be doing week to week: reinforcing the habits — explaining reasoning aloud, connecting ideas across units, reflecting on what was learned — that feed continuous assessment, rather than cramming content ahead of a date that does not exist in this programme.

The PYP exhibition is the closest thing to a capstone assessment, usually running through Term 2 or Term 3 of Year 6. Students choose a real-world issue — a DLF Wellington Estate group recently worked on urban water use, drawing directly on the neighbourhood's own borewell and water-tanker experience — research it in small groups over several weeks, and present findings plus a genuine action step to teachers, peers and parents. Tutoring support here looks less like content teaching and more like structuring the research process: narrowing an overly broad question, organising evidence into a coherent argument, and rehearsing the actual presentation, spread across the weeks before the deadline rather than crammed into the last one.

paragraphs: For most PYP families here, both formats work, and the honest answer is that home tutoring suits a five or six year old better while online closes most of the gap by Year 4 or 5. In person, a tutor can turn pages, point at a diagram and keep a wandering mind anchored to the table — something far harder to fake over a screen however good a tutor's online technique is. sections.heading: The Biggest Wrong Assumption Dundahera Parents Make About IB PYP
paragraphs: The instinct to help a struggling PYP student with more worksheets comes from somewhere reasonable — it worked for reading fluency or times tables in an older system. But the Primary Years Programme isn't built around isolated skill drills; it is built around transdisciplinary themes and units of inquiry, where a child is expected to ask their own questions, connect ideas across subjects, and reflect on how they learned something, not only whether they got it right. A tutor who defaults to worksheets is teaching to a different, older model of school than the one this child is actually in.

The genuine difficulty is that inquiry-based support is slower and less visible than drilling. There is no quiz score to point to after a session that proves a unit of inquiry landed. Progress looks like a child asking a sharper question than they did last week, or connecting an idea from a Sharing the Planet unit to something they noticed near Heritage City's own waste segregation bins. That is real progress, but it doesn't feel as reassuring as a worksheet covered in ticks, and a tutor who cannot explain that difference clearly will not hold a parent's confidence past the first month.

PYP is not a scaled-down version of a graded curriculum with exams removed. It is a different model of learning altogether, built around inquiry, the learner profile — traits like risk-taker, inquirer, reflective, caring — and six transdisciplinary themes repeated with growing depth each year. A tutor working within that model supports the questions a child is already asking rather than importing a new set of tasks from a different system entirely, and it is worth saying plainly that this approach can feel unfamiliar to a parent who grew up on a more content-heavy board.

There is also a version of this mistake that runs the other way: a parent who assumes PYP is 'just play' and needs no academic rigour at all. That is equally wrong. Inquiry-based learning still builds real reading, writing and numeracy skills, just through a different route — a child researching a How the World Works unit on simple machines is doing genuine science reasoning, not filling time. A tutor's job in Dundahera is often explaining this middle ground to parents as much as teaching the child, since both extremes undermine what PYP is actually trying to build.

sections.heading: What Do the IB PYP Units of Inquiry Actually Involve?
paragraphs: A unit of inquiry is a block of several weeks organised around one of six transdisciplinary themes — who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet — built around a central idea the class investigates through specific lines of inquiry, rather than a chapter of facts to memorise. Each theme repeats every year with growing depth, so a Year 2 How We Organise Ourselves unit and a Year 5 one on the same theme look genuinely different in complexity, not just in vocabulary.

Running alongside the six themes is the learner profile — ten attributes including inquirer, thinker, communicator and reflective, which schools report on formally, sometimes alongside or instead of the subject grades an older sibling might be used to. A tutor unfamiliar with this dual structure can end up reassuring a Dundahera parent about the wrong thing entirely, focusing on reading level when the school's actual report is flagging something about independence or reflection instead. Reading the real school report together, criterion by criterion, is usually more useful than a generic progress conversation.

Key concepts thread through every unit regardless of theme — form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective and responsibility — and a child is expected to use these explicitly when discussing their learning, not just absorb them passively. A tutor working on a How the World Works unit about simple machines, for instance, should be asking a child to explain the causation behind a lever working, not just have them label a diagram correctly. This is the layer of PYP that a generalist primary tutor, however capable otherwise, most often misses entirely.

The PYP exhibition in Year 6 is the programme's capstone: a self-directed, largely student-led inquiry into a real issue, presented to the school community, drawing on everything the learner profile and prior units built toward across five years. Families in Dundahera preparing for it often want more structured support than earlier years needed, which is reasonable — it is the one point in PYP that resembles a project with a hard deadline. But it still has to stay student-led to do what it is meant to do; a tutor who takes over the thinking defeats the exercise's purpose entirely.

Online is not unworkable for this age group, but it starts from a real handicap that a good tutor has to actively work against.

Even so, online genuinely earns its place for families in Dundahera further from where PYP-experienced tutors are based — say, needing someone to cross from DLF Phase 3 on a weekday evening through Udyog Vihar traffic. For supporting a specific unit of inquiry through read-aloud and discussion, a shorter, well-structured online session works close to as well as an in-person one, provided a parent stays nearby for the first several sessions to help with screen management, particularly for a child in the earlier PYP years.

A hybrid pattern suits many Dundahera families well: home sessions for the younger PYP years, when attention and comfort matter most, shifting toward a home-online mix as the child gets older and the exhibition approaches and the work turns more toward research and writing. Whichever mode is chosen, keeping sessions to thirty or forty minutes suits most PYP-age children better than a longer block, regardless of whether the tutor is sitting across the table or appearing on a screen.

One honest limitation: a hands-on inquiry activity — testing which materials are magnetic, building a simple model — is genuinely harder to run well online than a discussion-based unit, and no amount of good technique fully closes that gap for a young child. sections.heading: What Exactly Does the IB Primary Years Programme Teach?
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme teaches through six transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subjects — who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet — each explored through a unit of inquiry with its own central idea and lines of inquiry. A subject like maths or language is not taught in isolation; it is woven into whichever theme the class is exploring that term, which is precisely why a tutor unfamiliar with PYP structure can end up teaching against the unit rather than reinforcing it.

The learner profile, attributes such as inquirer, thinker, communicator and risk-taker, sits underneath every unit and shapes how work gets assessed, not as a separate subject but as a lens teachers apply throughout the year. A tutoring session that only targets content knowledge misses half of what PYP is actually building in a child, however strong the subject coaching itself might be on paper.

All of this converges in the Grade 6 PYP exhibition: a self-directed, small-group inquiry into a real-world issue, presented to the school community, drawing on research, action and reflection skills built up over the preceding five years of units. Palm Gardens groups have tackled issues ranging from waste management around Golf Course Extension Road construction sites to water conservation, choosing topics genuinely visible in their own neighbourhood rather than abstract textbook examples.

The exhibition is a different kind of challenge from anything earlier in the programme — students choose their own line of inquiry, manage their own timeline, and are expected to take initiative rather than follow instructions from a teacher or tutor. A tutor's role here is closer to a research coach than a subject teacher: helping structure the inquiry question, sourcing credible information appropriate to a ten or eleven year old, and keeping the project on schedule, without doing the thinking for the student at any stage.

sections.heading: Why Is IB PYP Genuinely Difficult to Tutor Well?
paragraphs: PYP is genuinely difficult to tutor well because the most common instinct — more worksheets, more repetition, more drilling of facts — actively works against how the programme assesses a child. The programme is built to measure how a student inquires, reasons and connects ideas across a theme, not how quickly they recall a memorised answer, so a tutor who responds to 'my child needs more practice' with a stack of worksheets is solving the wrong problem, even if test-style scores look temporarily better in the short term.

The better question is usually about process: can the child explain why they think something is true, not just state that it is? Can they connect an idea from one unit to something learned in a previous one, a specific skill PYP explicitly develops and assesses across the year? A tutor working well within PYP asks open questions, tolerates a wrong first answer without immediately correcting it, and lets a child work toward understanding rather than handing over the conclusion — slower in the moment, but it is what the programme actually measures.

This is genuinely harder to tutor than straightforward content delivery, and it is worth being honest about that limitation: inquiry-based tutoring takes longer to show visible results than drilling does, because the skill being built, independent reasoning, doesn't show up as a quick score jump the way a spelling test result does. Parents comparing PYP tutoring progress to a friend's child on a content-heavy curriculum are comparing two genuinely different kinds of development, and that comparison usually isn't a useful one to make.

There is a further layer many parents don't anticipate: a tutor also has to manage a child's own frustration with not being told the answer immediately, which some children find genuinely uncomfortable after years of a more direct teaching style at home. A skilled PYP tutor names that discomfort openly rather than pretending it doesn't exist, and gradually builds a child's tolerance for sitting with an unresolved question — a skill that pays off well beyond the Grade 6 exhibition, into Middle Years Programme (MYP) work later on.

From Grade 5 upward, particularly around exhibition year, a hybrid mix, home sessions for hands-on project work and online for research check-ins, tends to outperform either mode used alone.

We won't pretend one mode is always right, because it isn't. A child who concentrates well and genuinely enjoys screens can do perfectly well fully online through Grade 3 or 4, saving the scheduling friction of arranging a home visit around Sector 44 traffic on a weekday evening. A child who needs physical materials, counters, a whiteboard, a shared inquiry journal open on the table, usually does better in person, at least until the pattern of learning is established over the first month. Ask your matched tutor for an honest read after the first two sessions rather than deciding the mode in advance based on a general rule that may not fit your specific child.

sections.heading: Why the IB Primary Years Programme Curriculum Trips Up Bright Kids
paragraphs: PYP doesn't test recall the way a conventional syllabus does, and that is exactly why capable children sometimes plateau despite genuine ability. A child who is strong at maths or reading can still lose marks on a Unit of Inquiry summative task because the task assesses how they connect ideas across a transdisciplinary theme, say How the World Works, rather than whether they can define a term correctly on demand. Parents used to a more traditional Indian curriculum sometimes misread this as underperformance, when the child simply has not yet learned the specific skill of inquiry-based reasoning that PYP is actually built to teach, a skill that is trainable but rarely taught explicitly at home.

The six transdisciplinary themes, Who We Are, Where We Are in Place and Time, How We Express Ourselves, How the World Works, How We Organize Ourselves and Sharing the Planet, rotate across the year, and each genuinely demands a different kind of thinking from the child. A student strong on Where We Are in Place and Time, which rewards research and sequencing, can struggle noticeably on How We Express Ourselves, which rewards open-ended creative reasoning with no single correct structure. A tutor who treats every unit identically, running the same worksheet-style approach regardless of which theme is live, is not really teaching to the PYP at all, and a parent should expect a tutor to name which theme is currently active without being told.

The learner profile attributes, inquirer, thinker, communicator, principled, open-minded, caring, risk-taker, balanced and reflective, sound soft on paper, but schools around Huda City Centre assess against them formally and informally, often through a reflection journal entry graded alongside subject content. A child who is a strong thinker but a weak communicator will lose marks on a group reflection task even while holding the right answer in their head, simply because the task is measuring the communication attribute as much as the content. Good tutoring here means naming which specific attribute is the actual gap, rather than reviewing subject content again and hoping the next assessment happens to go better without addressing the real cause.

Take a concrete example from a recent Grade 4 unit under How the World Works: the central idea concerned energy transformation, and the summative task asked each child to design and explain a simple machine using at least two forms of energy, then reflect on which learner profile attributes they used during the design process. A child who built a technically sound machine but wrote a thin, one-line reflection lost marks on the communicator and reflective attributes despite nailing the science. This is precisely the kind of gap a subject-only tutor misses and a PYP-trained tutor catches immediately, and it tends to surface hardest in the two or three weeks before a school's mid-year reporting period, when reflection writing gets assessed alongside the content itself.

sections.heading: Inside the IB PYP Syllabus: Units of Inquiry to the Year 6 Exhibition
paragraphs: Each PYP year runs roughly six Units of Inquiry, one per transdisciplinary theme, each built around a central idea, a set of lines of inquiry, and the specific learner profile attributes the unit means to strengthen. A tutor working with your child should be able to name the current unit's central idea from memory rather than looking it up mid-session; that is the basic test of whether they understand what the school is actually doing that fortnight, rather than teaching generic maths and English content alongside it and hoping it happens to overlap with what the class is covering that week.

The Year 6 exhibition is the single biggest event on the PYP calendar and the one Huda City Centre parents ask about most by a wide margin. It is a self-directed, student-led inquiry into a real-world issue, presented to the school community, drawing on every learner profile attribute at once: research, collaboration, reflection and communication, all under a genuine deadline that does not move. Tutoring support here should look like coaching, not writing: helping the child narrow an overly broad topic, structure two or three workable lines of inquiry, and rehearse the actual presentation, while the thinking and the research stay entirely the child's own.

Numeracy and literacy still run underneath all of this, and PYP schools around Huda City Centre vary noticeably in how much weight they give each. Some, closer to a British-curriculum feel, push phonics and number fluency hard in the early years alongside the inquiry programme; others, including some running a fuller transdisciplinary model, lean almost entirely into inquiry from Grade 1 onward with skills woven into the unit itself rather than taught separately. Ask your school which model they follow before booking a tutor, because a tutor pitched for one approach can waste two or three weeks on the wrong balance of skills versus inquiry before anyone notices the mismatch.

Concretely, a Grade 2 Where We Are in Place and Time unit typically opens with a provocation, an object, image or question with no single right answer, moves through several weeks of guided and independent inquiry where the child researches a chosen angle, and closes with a summative task the school scores against three or four specific success criteria stated in the unit planner, criteria such as explaining how a place changes over time using two examples, or connecting a personal experience to a broader pattern. A tutor who has seen a real unit planner from a Huda City Centre school knows to ask for it in session one, because tutoring against the stated success criteria is measurably more useful than tutoring against a generic idea of what the unit might cover.

sections.heading: Why Does the IB PYP Curriculum Feel Harder at Home Than at School in Ireo Skyon?
paragraphs: The honest answer is that PYP is not primary school with a different name attached; it is built around inquiry, and a parent's instinct to sit down and simply 'help with homework' the way their own schooling worked can actually undercut what the programme is trying to build in a Grade 2 or Grade 3 child in Ireo Skyon. A worksheet answered correctly is not the same as a child who has genuinely investigated a question on their own, and a PYP teacher can usually tell the difference within a week from how the student talks about their own project rather than from the answer sheet itself.

The real difficulty for most families in this pocket is not the content itself, since PYP does not expect a seven-year-old to know advanced facts, but the format: open-ended units of inquiry that ask a child to plan their own line of investigation, reflect on what they found, and connect it back to a broader concept without a fixed answer key to check against. A child used to being told exactly what to do can find that genuinely disorienting at first, especially mid-year when a new unit opens and there is no worksheet to fall back on for reassurance.

Some children need very little outside support for PYP and genuinely do better when a parent steps back entirely, letting a stalled inquiry stay stalled for a day rather than rescuing it immediately with an answer. A tutor tends to be most useful when a child is consistently anxious about open-ended tasks, when a specific learner profile attribute like communicator or thinker is the visible bottleneck, or when English is not the home language and academic vocabulary in inquiry writing is the actual barrier rather than the ideas themselves. None of these situations means something has gone wrong at school; they simply mean a child needs a second, patient adult asking the same kind of question the classroom asks, rather than a shortcut to the answer.

A concrete example from a Grade 3 How We Organise Ourselves unit in this belt: the central idea concerned systems and community roles, and a child who could describe what a shopkeeper does but could not connect that to the broader idea of interdependence lost marks on the connecting-ideas criterion specifically, not on factual knowledge. This kind of gap tends to surface hardest in the fortnight before a school's term-end reporting period, when reflection writing gets checked alongside content, and a tutor unfamiliar with how PYP grades connection versus recall will often reteach the facts the child already knew instead of addressing the actual gap.

sections.heading: Inside the IB PYP Syllabus: From Units of Inquiry to the Year 6 Exhibition
paragraphs: The IB Primary Years Programme is organised around six transdisciplinary themes, Who We Are, Where We Are in Place and Time, How We Express Ourselves, How the World Works, How We Organise Ourselves, and Sharing the Planet, and each unit of inquiry sits under one of these, combining subjects rather than teaching them separately across the week. A tutor unfamiliar with this structure can end up reteaching maths or English in isolation, missing the connections the school unit is actually building between subjects that a standalone worksheet never shows. That gap is usually invisible to a parent checking homework for correctness, since the answers themselves can look fine while the connecting thread the school wants is entirely absent.

Running alongside the units of inquiry is the IB learner profile, attributes like inquirer, thinker, communicator and risk-taker, which schools use as much for reporting and reflection as for academic content itself. A tutor who understands this frames feedback the way the school does, so a child hears consistent language at home and in class instead of two different systems of praise and correction that can genuinely confuse a young learner about what is actually being asked of them. For a Grade 3 or 4 student in Ireo Skyon, this consistency alone often does more for confidence than any additional content coverage would.

For students in Year 6, the PYP exhibition is the culmination of the whole programme: a self-directed, collaborative inquiry project presented to the school community, drawing on research, reflection and communication skills built up over five previous years. Support here looks nothing like tutoring in the usual sense; it is closer to structured mentoring, helping a child manage a long-term project, research independently, and prepare to present, rather than teaching new content, and a tutor who tries to write or research the project themselves is working against what the exhibition is meant to assess.

Concretely, a typical exhibition timeline runs eight to ten weeks: two weeks choosing and narrowing a real-world issue tied to one of the six themes, three to four weeks of independent research and data gathering, two weeks structuring the presentation and gathering feedback from teachers or mentors, and a final week of rehearsal. A tutor mentoring this timeline in Ireo Skyon typically checks in weekly rather than running standard twice-a-week sessions, since the work between check-ins is meant to be the child's own, and over-scheduling a tutor into an exhibition project can quietly shift ownership away from the student without anyone intending it.

sections.heading: Why IB PYP Feels Different for Parents in M3M Heights
paragraphs: Parents in M3M Heights who grew up on chapter tests and unit exams often feel disoriented the first time they open their child's IB Primary Years Programme portfolio. There is no chapter to revise, no marks out of twenty to compare against last month. Instead there are approaches to learning skills, learner profile attributes like inquirer and reflective, and a running record of what the child asked, tried and changed their mind about. That is not a weaker system. It is a different one, and it asks a different kind of question at home: not 'what did you learn today' but 'what are you still wondering about'. Many families in M3M Heights, where both parents commute out along Golf Course Extension Road for work, simply do not have the evening hours to sit with that kind of open-ended question every day.

The risk is not that a child falls behind on facts. It is that a tutor, hired to 'help with PYP', quietly turns every unit of inquiry into a worksheet packet because worksheets are easier to grade and easier to show a parent as proof of progress. A Year 4 unit on how the world works can become a photocopied sheet on simple machines instead of an afternoon spent testing which lever arrangement lifts a schoolbag with the least effort. The second version is slower, messier, and harder to hold up as evidence at pickup time. It is also the version that actually matches what the Primary Years Programme is trying to build: a child who investigates before being told the answer, then reflects on what changed in their thinking.

Self-management is one of the five approaches to learning skill categories the Primary Years Programme tracks, and it is often the one M3M Heights households care about most, because it decides whether a child can start their own reading log or research folder without a parent standing over them. A tutor who only answers content questions misses this half of the job entirely. The more useful pattern, especially for a Year 3 or Year 4 child, is a short block of guided independence inside every session: five or ten minutes where the child plans the next step of an inquiry alone while the tutor watches rather than directs. Families who skip this step often find their child can perform well in a session but cannot start anything without an adult present.

One limitation is worth saying plainly. A home tutor cannot substitute for the classroom's own inquiry cycle, the tuning-in and finding-out stages a Programme of Inquiry unit runs through at school, because that happens in a group with a teacher who set the provocation. What a tutor in the M3M Heights pocket can do is extend it: ask the questions the class ran out of time for, help organise scattered notes into something the child can use later, and keep the reading and vocabulary moving between school terms. Booking a tutor to 'cover the syllabus' the way a Class 10 board tutor would is the wrong model here, and families who arrive expecting that usually adjust within the first few sessions once the shape of the programme becomes clear.

sections.heading: What Does the IB PYP Syllabus Actually Cover?
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme organises learning around six transdisciplinary themes rather than subjects in the traditional sense: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. Each year group runs through most or all of these as a Programme of Inquiry, usually one unit at a time across six to eight weeks, with literacy, mathematics and single subjects like art or physical education woven into the unit wherever the connection is genuine rather than forced. A tutor working with an M3M Heights family needs the current unit's central idea and lines of inquiry from the school, not a generic PYP outline, because two Year 4 classes running how the world works can build it around completely different content.

Take a concrete example. A Year 3 unit under how the world works might centre on forces and simple machines, with a central idea along the lines of 'forces can be used to make life easier'. The useful tutoring session is not explaining what a lever is from a textbook definition. It is setting up a broom handle and a brick at home, letting the child try lifting the brick three different ways, and asking them to explain which arrangement needed less effort and why, in their own words, before connecting that to the vocabulary of fulcrum and load. That single activity covers the content, the inquiry skill of testing a variable, and the reflection the child's portfolio will eventually ask for, in under twenty minutes.

Assessment in the Primary Years Programme does not produce a percentage or a letter grade the way a Class 8 ICSE report would. Schools report against the five approaches to learning categories, thinking, social, communication, self-management and research skills, alongside subject-specific criteria described in continuum language such as beginning, developing, proficient or extending. Parents who are used to a number to track often ask a tutor to translate this into something that feels comparable, and the honest answer is that it resists translation because it was designed to describe growth, not rank it. What does carry forward is real, though: the habits built in PYP research skills, especially notetaking and source use, are exactly what the Middle Years Programme expects a child to already have once they move into Year 7.

The programme's final year, Year 6, adds one requirement that shapes the entire year: the PYP exhibition, a student-led, collaborative inquiry into a real issue that the school usually runs across a full term, from choosing a topic in small groups through to presenting findings to the wider school community and parents. It draws on every transdisciplinary skill built over the previous five years at once, which is exactly why it tends to expose gaps in research or presentation skills that a straightforward exam never would. A tutor supporting a Year 6 child through this is not writing the project for them, since that defeats the entire purpose of a student-led exhibition. The realistic role is helping the child narrow an overly broad topic, structure their research notes, and rehearse explaining their findings out loud before the actual presentation.

sections.heading: What Does the IB PYP Curriculum Actually Involve?
paragraphs: The IB Primary Years Programme (PYP) is built around six transdisciplinary themes — who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet — each explored through a unit of inquiry that blends subjects together rather than teaching them separately, alongside the learner profile attributes that run through every unit regardless of topic.

Each unit of inquiry runs for several weeks and is framed around a central idea the whole class investigates together, using lines of inquiry as guiding sub-questions rather than a fixed list of facts to memorise. A Grade 3 unit under 'how the world works' might investigate simple machines through hands-on building, research and presentation, with the teacher assessing not just what the student learned but how they inquired — the questions they asked, the connections they made across subjects, and how they reflected on their own learning process along the way.

The learner profile — attributes like inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, and reflective — is not a side activity but woven into how every piece of work is discussed and assessed, which surprises parents used to a single subject-by-subject report card. A student can produce technically correct maths work and still receive feedback focused on collaboration or reflection, because the PYP evaluates the whole approach to learning, not isolated content mastery in the way a worksheet-based system does.

The PYP exhibition, usually completed in Year 6, is the programme's culminating event: students work in small groups over several weeks to research a real-world issue of their own choosing, connect it to a transdisciplinary theme, and present their findings to the school community, demonstrating everything the programme has built toward across the previous years. There is no formal written exam anywhere in the PYP; assessment is continuous, through observations, portfolios, rubrics and this final exhibition, which is exactly why a tutoring plan built around 'exam prep' misunderstands what actually needs support.

sections.heading: Why Supporting PYP Inquiry at Home Is Harder Than It Looks
paragraphs: The instinct most parents bring to any academic support is to make things clearer and more structured — a worksheet, a set of facts to memorise, a clear right answer to check against. That instinct works against the PYP's entire design, because the programme deliberately asks students to sit with open questions, follow their own curiosity within a unit of inquiry, and construct understanding rather than receive it, so a tutor who hands over neat answers is quietly undoing the skill the programme is trying to build.

This creates a genuine tension for a Mapsko Casa Bella family hiring outside academic support: too little structure and a student flounders, unsure what is actually expected of them within an open-ended unit; too much structure and the tutoring starts to resemble the rote-learning approach the PYP was designed to move away from. The right balance looks like guided questioning — asking a student what they already think and why, rather than telling them — which takes considerably more skill from a tutor than simply explaining a topic clearly.

A second difficulty is subject blending. A PYP unit under 'how we organise ourselves' might combine maths data-handling, persuasive writing and social studies research within a single inquiry, and a tutor used to teaching one subject at a time can struggle to hold that blend together coherently, defaulting instead to isolated maths drilling or isolated writing practice that misses the connecting thread the classroom teacher is actually building toward across the unit.

And there is a trade-off worth naming honestly here: a tutor who leans too hard into open-ended inquiry with a student who is genuinely behind on foundational reading or number skills can leave real gaps unaddressed, since inquiry-based learning assumes a baseline of skill the student uses to explore, not one still being built from scratch. For a student with a specific foundational gap, some direct, structured practice alongside the inquiry-based work is honestly necessary, not a compromise of PYP principles.

sections.heading: Inside the IB PYP Syllabus: Units of Inquiry and the Exhibition
paragraphs: The PYP is organised around six transdisciplinary themes, Who We Are, Where We Are in Place and Time, How We Express Ourselves, How the World Works, How We Organise Ourselves, and Sharing the Planet, with each unit of inquiry built around a central idea the class investigates together over several weeks. A tutor's job is not to re-teach a subject in the traditional sense; it is to help the child dig deeper into the current line of inquiry using the same open-ended, question-led approach the classroom itself uses, rather than substituting a worksheet-based method the school is deliberately moving away from.

The learner profile attributes, inquirer, thinker, communicator, and the rest, run underneath every unit, and schools increasingly expect a child to reflect on which attributes they used, not just what they learned in terms of raw content. This is where a lot of Nathupur parents feel unequipped to help at home, since it is a different kind of homework support than checking a maths worksheet for correct answers, and getting it wrong by turning reflection into rote answers tends to work against the child rather than for them in how the school actually scores the task.

By Year 6, the PYP exhibition becomes the centrepiece: a self-directed, collaborative inquiry project that students research and present largely on their own, with adults acting as guides rather than answer-givers throughout the process. A tutor experienced with the exhibition knows how to ask the next question without supplying the next fact, which is a harder discipline than it sounds and one that untrained homework help almost always gets wrong. Schools in this corridor generally expect visible independence in the final product, and a project that reads as adult-written tends to be flagged during the school's own review process.

Take a specific example from a Grade 3 How the World Works unit taught locally: the central idea concerned forces and motion, and the summative task asked children to build a simple device demonstrating one force, then write a reflection connecting it to a real-world example from their own life, a bicycle brake, a door hinge, a see-saw at a nearby park. Children who built a working device but could not make the real-world connection lost marks on the transfer-of-understanding criterion specifically, which is a different skill from the engineering itself and exactly the kind of gap a PYP-aware tutor is trained to catch.

sections.heading: Inside the IB PYP Syllabus: Units of Inquiry and the Year 6 Exhibition
paragraphs: PYP is organised around six transdisciplinary themes repeated across the years with rising depth: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. Each unit of inquiry sits under one of these themes, with a central idea, several lines of inquiry, and a set of learner profile attributes the school is watching for through the term, not only at its end.

By Year 6, this converges in the PYP exhibition, a student-led, collaborative inquiry into a real issue chosen largely by the students themselves and presented to the wider school community. It draws on everything built up over the preceding years, action, reflection, genuine inquiry skill, and is usually the first time a PYP student is asked to sustain an independent project over several weeks with minimal teacher scaffolding around them.

A tutor supporting exhibition preparation well acts more like a sounding board than an instructor, helping a Year 6 student narrow an overly broad topic, structure research, and reflect honestly on the action they actually took, rather than handing over content wholesale. Getting this balance wrong, doing too much of the thinking on the child's behalf, tends to produce a presentation that looks polished on the surface but scores poorly on genuine student agency, which examiners at this level notice quickly.

Unlike the IB Diploma Programme (DP), which reports on a 1 to 7 numeric scale, PYP reporting is criterion-based and narrative rather than a single figure, describing how a child is progressing against specific learning outcomes and approaches to learning within each unit. A parent comparing PYP reports against an older sibling's DP report card in the same household is comparing two genuinely different systems, not a simpler and a harder version of the same one.

sections.heading: Why Does IB PYP Resist Being Tutored Like a Normal Subject in Sispal Vihar?
paragraphs: PYP does not test facts the way most Indian schooling does, and that is exactly what makes it resist being tutored like a normal subject. A parent used to helping with times tables or a spelling list finds there is no equivalent worksheet for how the world works, one of the six transdisciplinary themes a Year 4 unit might explore over six weeks. The instinct is to fill that gap with something that feels productive, extra reading comprehension, extra sums, and that instinct, followed too far, quietly undermines what the programme is actually trying to build in a child.

Inquiry-based learning asks a child to form their own questions and follow evidence toward an answer, with the teacher, and the tutor, acting more as a guide than an answer key sitting on the shelf. That is a hard role for an adult who was taught the opposite way to hold consistently, session after session. It is tempting to just tell a curious seven-year-old the answer when they have been stuck for ten minutes, and sometimes that is fine, but a tutor who does it every time trains the child to stop asking and start waiting to be told.

There is also no compressed version of a PYP unit the way there might be a crash course before a board exam. A central idea has to be revisited across several weeks for a child to genuinely internalise it rather than repeat it once for a parent and forget it soon after. Families searching for an IB Primary Years Programme crash course in Gurugram are usually looking for something the programme's own structure does not really offer, and an honest tutor says so early rather than pretending otherwise.

The honest limitation worth naming here: not every family needs a tutor for this at all. A child who is naturally curious and whose unit of inquiry work at school is going fine probably does not need weekly sessions, occasional support before the Year 6 exhibition, or during a specific unit the child is struggling to connect with, is often genuinely enough. A good PYP tutor should say this rather than propose a standing weekly slot regardless of what the child actually needs that term.

sections.heading: Inside the PYP: Units of Inquiry, the Learner Profile and the Year 6 Exhibition
paragraphs: The PYP is organised around six transdisciplinary themes, who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet, and each year group works through several units of inquiry built from these themes rather than separate subjects taught in isolation. A Year 3 unit on how the world works might combine simple physics, a bit of writing, and a class discussion on sustainability inside one six-week block, unfamiliar territory for a tutor used to teaching maths and English as separate hours.

The learner profile, ten attributes like inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, runs alongside the academic content and shows up in how a child is expected to approach a task, not just what they know at the end of it. A tutor supporting a unit of inquiry is really supporting two things at once, the content itself, and the habit of approaching new information by questioning it rather than memorising it outright.

Everything builds toward the Year 6 exhibition, a self-directed inquiry project a student researches, plans and presents to the school community over several weeks, usually seen as the culmination of the entire PYP. It draws on every transdisciplinary theme the student has studied since Year 1, and a student who has never really practised independent research before Year 6 often struggles with the sheer scale of choosing and narrowing their own question.

Unlike the IB Diploma Programme's Higher Level (HL) and Standard Level (SL) subject grading on a 1 to 7 scale, PYP does not produce a numeric grade at any point; every report is narrative, tied to specific learning outcomes and the learner profile attributes observed that term. A tutor's job includes helping a first-time PYP parent read that narrative report accurately rather than searching it for a number that simply is not there.

sections.heading: Why IB PYP Support Goes Wrong Fast in South City 1
paragraphs: The most common assumption a South City 1 parent brings to tutoring for the International Baccalaureate (IB) Primary Years Programme (PYP) is that it should run like any other tuition: cover a topic, assign practice, check the answers. That model does not fit how the programme is actually built. A PYP class does not move through chapters; it investigates a central idea inside a broader unit of inquiry, with the child asking questions and gathering evidence rather than receiving facts from an adult. A tutor who brings CBSE or ICSE style drilling habits into that structure ends up working against what the school is doing, not alongside it, and most families in South City 1 only notice the mismatch after a full term of quiet frustration.

The clearest warning sign is a child who can recite what a unit covered but cannot explain why the class studied it or what question it was actually trying to answer. That is memorisation standing in for inquiry, and because PYP report cards are narrative rather than graded, there is no falling percentage to flag the problem early. A parent who occasionally asks what were you curious about today, rather than what did you learn, tends to catch this drift months before a school conference would surface it. The distinction sounds small. It changes what a good tutoring session actually looks like from the inside.

Take a central idea like systems help societies function, a typical how we organise ourselves unit. A drill-minded tutor turns this into vocabulary to memorise: define a system, list three examples. A tutor working the way PYP intends instead asks the child to trace one real system — the traffic signal near South City 1's own market, say — and work out what happens when one part fails. The second approach takes longer and produces less that looks like finished homework at the end of an hour. It also builds the actual skill the programme is assessing, which the first approach does not, however tidy the notebook looks afterward.

None of this means PYP has no content to learn. Spelling, number sense and reading fluency still need deliberate practice, and a tutor who treats every session as pure open-ended inquiry, with no skill-building at all, is avoiding one job to look faithful to another. The two belong together: skill practice in service of a question the child actually cares about, not skill practice as the entire session, and not inquiry with no scaffolding underneath it. This balance matters most in the years building up to the Year 6 exhibition, when a student is suddenly expected to drive independent research and finds out, often too late, whether that muscle was ever built.

sections.heading: What Does the IB PYP Curriculum Actually Cover?
paragraphs: The IB Primary Years Programme organises learning around six transdisciplinary themes: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. Each unit of inquiry sits under one theme and is built around a central idea explored through open, teacher-guided questions, revisited at increasing depth as a child moves from Year 1 through Year 6. There is no textbook chapter to point to and no single syllabus code the way an older sibling's IB Diploma Programme (DP) subject would have, which is exactly what confuses most South City 1 parents new to the programme.

Each unit also develops Approaches to Learning skills — research, communication, self-management, social and thinking skills — assessed alongside the content itself, not as an afterthought bolted onto a report card. A child can understand a topic reasonably well and still be marked down on the research or communication side if their process was disorganised, a distinction most parents do not realise is being tracked at all until a conference makes it explicit. This is one reason a PYP tutor's job differs from a subject tutor's: half the work is the thinking process, not the content sitting on top of it.

Running alongside every unit is the learner profile — ten attributes including inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, and reflective — which teachers comment on almost as often as they comment on subject content. A tutor working with a South City 1 family should be able to name which learner profile attributes a given unit is actually building, because vague praise like doing well is not useful feedback for a parent trying to judge real progress. Ask a prospective tutor this directly: which attribute is this unit developing, and how would you know if my child were struggling with it rather than just quiet.

By Year 6, all of this converges in the PYP exhibition — a collaborative, student-led inquiry project chosen and researched largely by the students themselves and presented to the wider school community, typically over several weeks in Term 2 or Term 3 depending on the school's own calendar. It is the single biggest test of whether the earlier years actually built independent inquiry skill, and families who start exhibition preparation from zero in Year 6 itself usually find it a steeper climb than the one term they budgeted for. There is no equivalent of IB Diploma Programme past paper practice here — PYP has no exam to drill for, which is precisely why the exhibition carries so much weight instead.
